tagline: Old turnpike routes connect a courthouse village with rural Scotland
intro: Routes 203 and 14 link a Shetucket River crossing, Windham Center’s green and the rural country toward Scotland. Route 203 between Route 32 and Route 14 is designated scenic, as is a 4.4-mile section of Route 14 between Windham and Scotland. Just east of Windham Center, Scotland Road descends between stone walls, with fields on both sides.

Before the turnpikes, Rochambeau’s French troops used Scotland Road in 1781 on their way to Yorktown and again on their return in 1782, when they camped beside it. These roads retain parts of two turnpike routes. The Windham Turnpike, chartered in 1799, ran through Scotland along what is now Route 14. The southern part of Route 203 belonged to the Windham and Mansfield Turnpike, chartered the next year. Both modern route numbers date to the state’s 1932 renumbering.

Start in South Windham at Route 32, cross the Shetucket on Route 203 and continue north to Windham Center. The green is bordered by a Congregational church and the former Windham Bank, converted to a library. Take Route 14 east as Scotland Road toward Scotland, where Huntington Road passes the Samuel Huntington Birthplace. In Scotland, the route also takes the name Palmer Road and briefly shares its course with Route 97.

moments.title: Windham Center
moments.text: Windham Center’s green is bordered by the original Greek Revival Windham Bank, built in 1832 and converted to the Windham Free Library in 1896. The village became the county seat in 1726 and prospered from courthouse business. Its bank once issued notes bearing a frog sitting on an upturned dead frog, a reference to the town’s 1754 frog scare. The bank used that image on denominations from one to ten dollars until the 1870s. The green also has a Congregational church, a post office, houses and a former inn, with four roads leading out toward the surrounding country.

moments.title: Samuel Huntington Birthplace
moments.text: The long rear roof of the Huntington house slopes to the first floor, giving it its saltbox shape. Built in the first quarter of the eighteenth century, it was Samuel Huntington’s birthplace in 1731. He later signed the Declaration of Independence and served as Connecticut’s governor. Inside, a narrow winding stair stands in front of the central chimney, with public rooms on either side. The woodwork and plaster are almost entirely original. Local citizens formed the Governor Samuel Huntington Trust in 1994; restoration, rehabilitation and archaeological work followed, investigating how the property was used.
moments.notice: The rear roof slopes down to the first floor behind a large central chimney.

moments.title: Scotland
moments.text: Scotland carries a name chosen by Isaac Magoon to commemorate his ancestral home. He purchased 1,950 acres from Windham in 1700; Scotland became a separate town in May 1857. It remains predominantly rural, with agriculture its principal industry. The D’Elia Antique Tool Museum, established in the public library building in 2005, holds more than 1,200 antique woodworking planes, with examples dating to the middle of the eighteenth century. Town meetings remain its form of government, with a board of selectmen, continuing a civic practice alongside the town’s farming economy.
